**AI coding research brief | November 13, 2026**

**1. [ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13246) · November 9**

Before trusting a verifier to grade a worker, check whether it can tell a valid alternative from an incomplete fix. On 100 expert-authored tasks across 87 repositories, every grader had to give full credit to a reference patch and zero to both an untouched checkout and an inert edit. For 35 tasks, an alternative valid solution also had to pass; for 42, a deliberately incomplete or no-op patch had to score low. Those controls test both ways a reviewer can be wrong. The suite was selected for difficulty, and the paper did not test whether adding controls improves a production coordinator.

**2. [SWE-Time: Benchmarking Temporal Repository Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12083) · November 9**

A commit log and a symptom report can leave a debugging worker without the evidence it needs. Across a benchmark of 1,661 cases from 65 repositories, the authors tested both tracing regressions backward and predicting changes forward. In a controlled backward comparison, the score for identifying the first bad commit fell from 62% to 28% when historical source and diffs were removed but the report, commit sequence and metadata remained. This measures localization, not successful repair.

**Quadratus experiment:** Give one worker a last-known-good revision, the symptom and scoped diffs; give another the same symptom and commit metadata. Under equal budgets, measure first-bad-commit accuracy, verified repairs and time spent reading history.

**3. [FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13241) · November 9**

FlowPlan describes a repair as a change to a function’s control or data flow, then rebuilds the graph after editing to check what actually changed. On 158 SWE-bench Pro tasks, Haiku 4.5 used 46–47% of baseline tokens; Sonnet 5 used 72–76%. Across the study’s configurations, resolution rates showed no statistically significant difference. Most savings came from fewer cache reads, so token reductions cannot be read as equivalent dollar savings or as proof of equal accuracy.

**Quadratus experiment:** For localized repairs, have the planner hand the implementer a before-and-after flow sketch. Let the verifier compare it with the actual change and run independent behavior tests. Compare with prose plans on cost per verified fix, counting graph construction and cached tokens at their actual prices.

**4. [Do They Do as They Are Told? Investigating Coding Agents’ Adherence to Explicit Instructions in Context Files](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13709) · November 10**

Among 2,053 repository instructions measurable from commits, 54.4% were satisfied on every applicable commit and 37.3% on none. That makes an overall compliance score a poor way to discover which rule a coordinator can trust. Only 13.8% of candidate instructions yielded an observation; a spot check also found roughly three in ten accepted measurement scripts implemented their rule incorrectly. These are estimates from artifacts, not evidence of what a worker read.

**Quadratus experiment:** Audit a few consequential rules individually, such as whether a worker stayed within assigned paths. Hand-check the measurement against labeled diffs before relying on it. Record “not observable” separately from “violated.”

**Try first: calibrate the verifier before it grades workers.** On held-out archived tasks, prepare a known-good patch, a different valid implementation and a plausible partial fix. Hide their identities. Compare ordinary review against a verifier calibrated on separate examples, using the same model and total budget. Measure false acceptance of partial fixes and false rejection of valid alternatives separately. This would tell Quadratus whether its review step improves decisions before it spends more on reviewers.
